```text
Peak Poker Performance

Exercise
After we’re done with our mental work, our next daily ritual should be to
participate in some form of exercise. Even moderate amounts of exercise
have been shown to boost energy, enhance health, improve emotional
well-being, and strengthen focus. I’ll have a lot more to say about exer-
cise in a future chapter, but for now realize that even very modest
amounts of exercise provide anti-depressant and anti-anxiety effects and
improve focus. A little movement goes a long way. In fact, exercise is like
a little bit of Prozac and a little bit of Ritalin rolled into one!

Reading
Reading is next on Elrod’s list. He makes the case that reading is a great
way to transform ourselves by learning from experts. In the poker realm
we also have access to a number of video training sites, which in my opin-
ion could be substituted for reading. Think about what content you need
to learn, study, read, or watch to set yourself up for success. Make con-
suming some of your study materials each day a regular habit. The key is
to have a daily system for thinking about or learning new ideas.

Scribing
Elrod’s term for writing is “scribing,” and part of his system entails spend-
ing time writing in a journal. You could make notes on your goals, the ac-
tions you are taking to reach those goals, books you want to read, videos
you want to watch, mental game strategies to try, or anything else re-
lated to the improvement of your game. Taking a few minutes to write
each day is a good way to stay on track.
   If you follow Elrod’s system, you’ll be spending an hour or so each
morning on personal development. Imagine what a difference you would
see if you employed this system over the next month or two. Over a year,
your changes could be dramatic. I have countless clients who are using a
systems approach much like this, and they are universally reporting being
more energized and productive since starting morning routines. I’m get-
ting reports from players who are consistently putting in more volume
```

```text
                                                  Systematizing Success

and seeing increases in time on their A game. It’s fine to tweak the system
to fit your needs. What’s important is that you have a morning routine
that helps you get off to a good start.

Bookend Your Days
Darren Hardy, the author of The Compound Effect, goes one step farther
and says we need to bookend our days with world-class routines. He ar-
gues that it is not always within our abilities to control what happens to
us during the day, but we can almost always control how our day starts
off and how it ends. If you want to be world class at anything, you need
to build your performance around world class systems. What are the
things you are willing to start and end your days with in order to become
a more consistent poker player?
    Often our nighttime rituals set us up for success or failure the next
day. Think about some systems you can implement in the evening that will
virtually guarantee you a smooth start the next day. Many players get
good results by meditating before bed. You might also take some time to
create some plans for the next day. One of my clients actively does a
“digital sundown” where he closes electronic items by a certain time so
that he gets a better night’s sleep. Better yet, find someone who has had
a level of success that you wish to emulate and see if you can find out
what they do to make their days start and end smoothly.

Small Choices Add Up: The Compound Effect
Darren Hardy describes his formula for success; it fits neatly into the sys-
tems ideology:


         Small, Smart Choices + Consistency + Time =
         Radical Difference


  He refers to this principle as the compound effect. You can reap large
rewards from making a series of small, smart choices each day. These
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

choices are so small that they may almost seem insignificant. What makes
them so effective is that they add up to massive results over time.
    Imagine how much additional knowledge you would have if you de-
voted an hour each day to watching and taking notes on poker videos.
What if you only devoted a half hour to it? Over the course of a year or
two imagine how much further ahead you would be than the player who
does nothing. There is a saying, “Your day is your week is your month is
your year.” How we spend our days is very indicative of how our year will
turn out. If you want different outcomes, you have got to change what
you’re doing – but the changes don’t have to be large.
    Hardy says that the only path to success is through following a contin-
uum of mundane, unsexy, unexciting, and sometimes difficult daily disci-
plines. It’s not always fun to do the things that need to be done to achieve
our goals. To top it all off, the greater the challenge we have set for our-
selves, the more rigorous our routines need to be.
    Don’t forget that there is another side to this coin. As you are building
your systems of actions and activities, don’t forget to make a list of all the
things you are going to stop doing. If there are behaviors or activities that
are not helping you get what you want, get rid of them immediately if not
sooner! It might be eye opening to think about and list out the answers to
these questions:

     ♠ What are the things that help me achieve success?
     ♠ What are the things that are getting in the way of my achieving
        success?


   Jeff Olson discusses a similar concept to the compound effect, which
he calls the “slight edge.” In The Slight Edge he says that the things that
take us from failure to success are simple. They are so simple that it’s
easy to overlook them, but successful people actually do them! Investing
a few dollars each week or exercising for a few minutes each day are the
types of tiny behaviors that can have massive results over time. He calls
these habits simple daily disciplines.
```

```text
                                                                                      Systematizing Success

   Olson goes further by discussing the role that preparedness plays in
luck. He says that being prepared creates opportunities and preparedness
comes from doing those simple, constructive, positive actions over and
over. Forget about the “big break.” Look instead for your break to come
after some period of accumulation of slight edge effort.

The 5% Solution
Steve Chandler is a systems expert who talks about how it can be difficult
to make rapid, dramatic changes. Instead he advocates a systems ap-
proach where you look for very small incremental improvements on the
order of 5%. He says that while it may be hard to figure out how to over-
haul your entire game, it is relatively easy to think of ways where you
could improve by 5%. Try it out and see if you can come up with some
ideas. Here are a few prompts to get you started. Try to come up with a
few strategies for each one.
   What would I need to do (or stop doing) to improve my preflop play by
5%:

   ♠ .......................................................................................................
   ♠ .......................................................................................................
   ♠ .......................................................................................................

  If I were 5% more prepared for today’s session I would:

   ♠ .......................................................................................................
   ♠ .......................................................................................................
   ♠ .......................................................................................................

  You can apply this line of thinking to anything you want to change or
improve. Your goal is to improve your situation by 5%.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Track Your Behaviors
The most effective way to change your life is to start tracking your be-
haviors because awareness is always the first step to changing them. If
you want better finances, track every penny you spend. If you want to
improve your play from the blinds, track every hand you play from those
positions (along with the results). If you tend to procrastinate, start
tracking your time. Want to improve your diet? Track every single thing
you put into your mouth. If we become conscious of every choice we
make in those spots, we’ll get dialed in very quickly. It becomes incredibly
easy to see what we need to change.
   I hope that you are starting to see that the only thing that stands be-
tween you and what you want is your behavior. You can make very small
changes and as long as they are consistent they will make all of the differ-
ence over time. If you are doing things that are blocking your path to suc-
cess, replace them with something better.

Gaining Momentum
It can be difficult to get started with new systems and processes. It’s
Newton’s First Law – objects at rest tend to stay at rest unless acted
upon. Objects in motion tend to stay in motion unless acted upon. What
we must do then is get started. In The Compound Effect (2011), Hardy
offers a five-step strategy for increasing momentum:

     ♠ Start making new choices based on our most valued goals and
        desires.
     ♠ Put these choices to work by enacting positive behaviors.
     ♠ Repeat these new behaviors enough times that they become
        habits.
     ♠ Build routines into your daily disciplines.
     ♠ Stay consistent over a very long period of time.
```

```text
                                                  Systematizing Success

   Jason Selk, sports psychologist and the author of Executive Toughness,
says the key is to make gradual improvement over time. Progress accel-
erates when we emphasize improvement over perfection. By taking
things slowly and creating systems that lead to small, incremental wins,
we take the pressure for perfection off. If you don’t know what to do
next to get your momentum kick started, just ask yourself, “What’s one
thing I can do to make this better?” By committing yourself to staying fo-
cused on what you want and being relentless in your pursuit of it, you will
stay in control and make your success more likely. All it requires is that
you set up your routines to make success more likely than not.

Continuous Improvement Through Kaizen
Kaizen is a Japanese management strategy that focuses on small, contin-
ual improvement over a long period of time. It was promoted rather vig-
orously to American manufacturing companies in the 1940s by a statisti-
cian named Dr. W. Edwards Deming. Deming was convinced that little
changes could brilliantly accelerate America’s manufacturing capacity, and
those companies that implemented his strategies did attain amazing re-
sults over the ensuing decades. More recently, kaizen has been touted as
a means by which people can make changes and enjoy improvements.
   If you’ve had trouble making change, you can be comforted with the
knowledge that most people don’t do well with radical all-or-nothing
strategies. It is common to fall off the wagon rather quickly or to give up
on lofty goals at the first sign of difficulty. It can be hard to stay moti-
vated and if your motivation fails, you are stuck relying on willpower,
which is limited by many factors (decision fatigue, tiredness, stress, hun-
ger, etc.). If sticking to performance enhancing strategies has been diffi-
cult for you, consider trying a strategy of continual improvement.
   John Wooden, one of the greatest basketball coaches of all time,
taught kaizen-like practices to his players. He said,

      When you improve each day, eventually big things occur. When
      you improve conditioning a little each day, eventually you have
```

```text
  Dr. Robert Maurer wrote a book on using kaizen to make individual
change, One Small Step Can Change Your Life (2004), in which he sug-
gests a set of steps you can use to continuously improve:

     ♠ Ask small questions.
     ♠ Think small thoughts.
     ♠ Take small actions.
     ♠ Solve small problems.
     ♠ Bestow small rewards.

   He says that your brain loves questions and sees them as puzzles to be
solved. If you pose small puzzles to your brain regularly, you will start to
come up with creative ideas and solutions that you can use in your sys-
tems for improvement. How would you answer the following questions:

     ♠ If poker were my first priority, what would I be doing differently
        today?
     ♠ What is one way that I can remind myself to drink more water
        while I play?
     ♠ How could I incorporate just a few minutes of exercise into my
        day?

   If you chew on these ideas for a time, I bet you’ll come up with some
creative ideas to implement.
```

## PDF page 80

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/Peak%20Poker%20Performance.pdf#page=80)

```text
                                                       Systematizing Success

change of some kind. Basically, you spend very small amounts of time
each day imagining yourself engaging in new tasks – especially those that
are difficult. Many professional athletes, including Michael Jordan and
Jack Nicklaus, make use of imagery techniques to continuously improve.
There is no reason why you can’t use them as well.
    Taking small actions is at the heart of kaizen. Maurer makes the case
(similar to that made by Guise and Fogg in the previous chapter) that you
are most likely to accrue successes if you take actions that are so small
that they almost seem silly. Let’s say you want to go to bed earlier. A kai-
zen strategy would be to go to bed one minute earlier each night. He says
these systems work because they trick your brain into thinking “this
change is so tiny that it’s no big deal.” You might be thinking that such
small steps will get you nowhere fast, but once you get your system go-
ing, change can end up being pretty rapid. The first step is rarely the last.
To get into action on any task simply ask: what will be my first small step?
    Solving small problems is a very effective system. Hindsight is gener-
ally 20/20, but if you can train yourself to see warning signs earlier, you
can save yourself a lot of trouble. Think back to a major mistake you made
in your last playing session. Were there any small signs along the way that
were indicators that things were not going to turn out as you wanted?
Did you ignore any signs? Did you have options at your disposal that you
could have used, but didn’t?
    The goal in looking for small mistakes is not to get angry with yourself.
It is to raise your awareness; if you look for small things to correct after
each playing session, you will reduce your mistake frequency. Whenever
you come up with a mistake or problem, immediately think about what
small step you could take to solve it. You should also ask yourself if this
mistake is part of a larger issue. If it is, get to work on it.
    Finally, the kaizen philosophy includes the notion that small rewards are
optimal for increasing intrinsic motivation. When you enact your systems,
give yourself a little reward. It could be a simple “atta boy” or “atta girl” or it
could be a bite of chocolate or practically anything else you can think of.
The key is that you reward yourself regularly as you are making progress.
```
